candidates.title: Treat low-frequency operands as a failure mode in arithmetic agents
candidates.rule: For agent workflows that depend on LLM-computed arithmetic or unit conversion, route the computation to an external calculator/tool rather than relying on in-context few-shot answers, especially when operands are uncommon; adding more shots does not remove the frequency bias.
candidates.passage: even though the model gets more accurate, the improvements focus on more frequent instances of the task
candidates.finding: Authors measured that performance gaps generally grew with more shots (e.g., GPT-J addition-# gap 18.1 at k=2 to 38.5 at k=16). The tool-use recommendation is our extrapolation; the paper did not test calculators or tool routing.
candidates.conditions: Plain Q/A prompt templates, no chain-of-thought, no tools, k up to 16 shots; models from 2021-2022.
candidates.limitations: Tool routing was never compared in the paper; the frequency effect may be weaker in newer, larger, or CoT/tool-trained models. One easy task (decade-to-year) reached 100% with no gap, so blanket tool routing may be unnecessary for trivial conversions.
candidates.validation_test: Build a task mix with matched-difficulty arithmetic over frequent vs rare operands and compare end-to-end agent accuracy with direct model computation vs calculator tool calls at equal token budget.

reason: The paper measures a term-frequency performance gap on numerical reasoning tasks across GPT-Neo/GPT-J models, which supports an evaluation-design rule (report frequency-stratified accuracy) and a deployment caution (don't trust aggregate few-shot arithmetic accuracy for rare operands). Other content is descriptive or related work.
